name: sse-popcount
baseline: scalar hardware POPCNT instruction loop (cpu / builtin-popcnt via __builtin_popcountll), plus lookup-table and bit-parallel scalar versions
workload: Population count over 32 B to 4096 B buffers, repeated a fixed number of times (5 runs), times reported in seconds per procedure; AVX2/AVX-512 Harley-Seal and PSHUFB-lookup versus scalar POPCNT.
claimed_speedup: Cascade Lake Xeon Gold 6240 at 4096 B: avx512-harley-seal 0.04826 s versus cpu (POPCNT loop) 0.17391 s and builtin-popcnt 0.25037 s, about 3.6x and 5.2x (derived from page data); avx2-harley-seal 0.09748 s versus cpu 0.17391 s, about 1.8x (derived from page data). At 32-256 B the POPCNT loop wins (avx512-harley-seal 2.99407 s versus cpu 0.30912 s at 32 B).
compiler_and_flags: GCC 8.3.0 (crosstool-NG 1.24.0) for the Cascade Lake run; Makefile in repo sets -std=c++17 -O2 -mpopcnt, plus -mavx2 or -mavx512bw per target (current Makefile; the result files were generated earlier, so flags per run are inferred from the Makefile, not printed in the result file)
hardware: Cascade Lake Xeon Gold 6240 @ 2.6 GHz (AVX512BW), generated 2021-02-24; the repo also has Haswell i7-4770, Skylake i7-6700, Skylake-X, Cannon Lake i3-8121U, Sandy Bridge-E, Westmere, Bulldozer and ARM result files
stars_or_usage: 357 stars; companion repo of the Muła, Kurz and Lemire paper 'Faster Population Counts Using AVX2 Instructions' (arXiv 1611.07612, Computer Journal 2018)
tradeoffs: x86-specific sample programs (SSSE3/AVX2/AVX-512BW/VBMI), not a packaged library; needs a CPU with the matching extension and loses to the POPCNT instruction below roughly 512 B; kimwalisch/libpopcnt is the packaged, runtime-dispatched version of the same ideas.
caveats: Result files are old (Haswell file generated 2016-03-26, GCC 5.3.0; Cascade Lake 2021, GCC 8.3.0). Haswell file (https://github.com/WojciechMula/sse-popcount/blob/master/results/haswell/haswell-i7-4770-gcc5.3.0-avx2.rst) shows avx2-harley-seal 0.11145 s versus cpu 0.19857 s at 4096 B (about 1.8x, derived from page data) and a loss at 32-256 B. Baseline is the scalar POPCNT instruction, which is a strong baseline, not naive scalar code. Authors of the repo are the paper authors (first-party for the paper, but the code and tables are public and reproducible). Paper abstract (search snippet only, arXiv not opened) says the vectorized approach can be twice as fast as the dedicated instruction.
found_via: WebSearch: '"Faster Population Counts Using AVX2 Instructions" Muła Kurz Lemire Harley-Seal speed github sse-popcount'; then github.com/WojciechMula/sse-popcount results directory and github.com/topics/popcount

name: positional-popcount
baseline: pospopcnt_u16_scalar_naive (portable scalar C, auto-vectorized by GCC) and pospopcnt_u16_scalar_naive_nosimd
workload: Positional population count (count of set bits at each of 16 bit positions) over arrays of 16-bit values, 128 to 65536 values, 1 million simulated FLAG fields repeated 1000 times on one core.
claimed_speedup: pospopcnt_u16_avx512_harley_seal is 16.28x faster than the auto-vectorized scalar naive version at 65536 values (6.43x at 4096, 9.41x at 8192) and 138.71x faster than the no-SIMD naive version at 65536 values; AVX-512 adder forest 4.96x at 2048; at 128 values the Harley-Seal version is 0.52x (slower). README also states about 50 GB/s (about 0.120 cycles per 16-bit integer) with AVX-512.
compiler_and_flags: gcc (GCC) 7.3.1 20180303 (Red Hat 7.3.1-5); Makefile OPTFLAGS -O3 -march=native, CFLAGS -std=c99, bench built with -std=c++11
hardware: Cannon Lake Core i3-8121U for the speedup table; cycles and MB/s tables also give Sky Lake Xeon W-2104 and Haswell Xeon E5-2697 v3
stars_or_usage: 57 stars; code of the paper 'Efficient Computation of Positional Population Counts Using SIMD Instructions' (Klarqvist, Muła, Lemire, arXiv 1911.02696)
tradeoffs: Fastest variants need AVX-512 (Cannon Lake / Skylake-X class); SSE and AVX2 fallbacks are included; experimental repo, the README points production users to libalgebra.h; small arrays (under about 512 values) can be slower than the scalar path.
caveats: Speedup table baseline is the compiler auto-vectorized scalar version at -O3 -march=native, which is a fair baseline; the larger 138.71x figure is against a deliberately non-vectorized baseline. Results are from one 2019-era laptop-class CPU for the speedup table. Peer-review status of the paper not verified here (arXiv not reachable). libalgebra (same author) reuses these kernels, so the two entries overlap.
found_via: github.com/topics/popcount page (positional-popcount listed); cross-checked with WebSearch result for 'Faster Population Counts Using AVX2 Instructions' lineage

name: libalgebra
baseline: naive unvectorized scalar code (popcount_scalar_naive_nosimd, pospopcnt_u16_scalar_naive_nosimd, set-algebra *_scalar_naive_nosimd)
workload: Popcount, positional popcount and bitmap set-algebra cardinalities (AND/OR/XOR) over arrays of 4 to 1048576 64-bit words, in CPU cycles per word on an AVX512BW machine.
claimed_speedup: Popcount 16.4x at 1024 words, 21x at 8192 words, 4.2x at 1048576 words; set algebra 15.3x at 1024 word pairs, 13.7x at 8192; positional popcount up to 138.71x at 65536 values; slower or equal for tiny inputs (0.8x at 4 word pairs).
compiler_and_flags: gcc (GCC) 8.2.1 20180905 (Red Hat 8.2.1-3); optimization flags not confirmed (Makefile not found at the repo root)
tradeoffs: Header-only C/C++ library using POPCNT, SSE4.2, AVX2, AVX512BW and NEON; tested with GCC, Clang and MSVC per the README.
caveats: Baseline is a deliberately naive, non-SIMD scalar loop rather than the POPCNT instruction or __builtin_popcountll, so speedups overstate the gain over a tuned scalar loop (sse-popcount shows only 1.8x to 5x over the POPCNT instruction). Single machine, optimization flags not shown, performance upper bound (aligned, cache-resident data). Shares kernels with positional-popcount, so likely a near-duplicate.
found_via: Opened from the positional-popcount README ('For production applications please use libalgebra.h') found via github.com/topics/popcount

name: FastNoise2
baseline: FastNoise Lite (scalar C++), FastNoise legacy, libnoise, stb_perlin
workload: Million noise points generated per second, 2D and 3D Value, Perlin, Simplex and Cellular noise, FastNoise2 AVX2 build against scalar noise libraries.
claimed_speedup: 3D: Value 494.49 versus 64.13 (FastNoise Lite), Perlin 261.10 versus 47.93, Simplex 268.44 versus 36.83 (OpenSimplex in FastNoise Lite), Cellular 52.43 versus 12.49 million points/s; 2D: Value 776.33 versus 114.01, Perlin 624.27 versus 92.83, Simplex 466.03 versus 71.30, Cellular 194.30 versus 39.15. Ratios of roughly 4x to 8x (derived from page data).
hardware: Intel 7820X @ 4.9 GHz, Windows 10 x64, AVX2 build
tradeoffs: Node-graph API aimed at generating arrays of noise with fused SIMD pipelines (the README argues scalar combination of separately generated arrays defeats SIMD); several SIMD feature sets are supported; a 2026-10-10 commit fixed 4D Simplex domain-warp output differing between SIMD feature sets, so outputs can vary slightly across instruction sets; not the same noise function as FastNoise Lite in every column (Simplex versus OpenSimplex).
caveats: Benchmark harness is the public Auburn/NoiseBenchmarking repo (same author, submodules for each library; opened the repo page only, no results file), so reproducibility rests on that harness; compiler is old (clang-cl 10) on Windows; comparison is AVX2 bulk generation versus mostly scalar single-point libraries, so the gain mixes SIMD and API-shape effects. The project also keeps continuous benchmarks on an auburn.github.io page that was not reachable here.
found_via: github.com/topics/simd-optimization and topics pages (FastNoise2 listed under simd/avx512 topics); README Performance section opened via raw.githubusercontent.com

name: pure_simd
baseline: scalar C++ version of the same integer shader loop (BM_shader_scalar_shader)
workload: Per-pixel integer shader (99 iterations of modulo-heavy integer arithmetic per pixel) over a screen buffer, pure_simd_shader instantiated with vector sizes 1 to 128.
claimed_speedup: Scalar 103 ms; pure_simd vector size 8: 28.0 ms, 16: 16.2 ms, 32: 12.5 ms, 64: 10.9 ms (about 9.5x faster than scalar, derived from page data); size 128 is 158 ms, slower than scalar.
compiler_and_flags: clang++ 9.0 -O3 -march=native (CMakeLists sets -O3 -march=native, C++17), Google Benchmark via Conan
tradeoffs: Header-only, experimental ('first baby step'), interfaces change; vector sizes beyond the hardware register width are unrolled lanes, and an oversized unroll hurts the instruction cache (size 128 is 15x slower than size 64 in its own table).
caveats: A single toy workload (one shader) on one laptop CPU; the scalar baseline is the author's own loop with the same flags, and the README does not say whether GCC or clang auto-vectorized it; numbers are means of 10 iterations. No comparison with Highway, xsimd, Eigen or std::simd.
found_via: github.com/topics/simd-library page (pure_simd listed, 233 stars); README benchmark section and CMakeLists.txt opened via raw.githubusercontent.com

name: ISPC (Intel SPMD Program Compiler)
baseline: scalar C/C++ code (README does not name the baseline compiler or workload)
workload: SPMD kernels compiled to SIMD units; README states a general speedup range over scalar code, no specific workload.
claimed_speedup: 'frequently provides a 3x or more speedup on architectures with 4-wide vector SSE units and 5x-6x on architectures with 8-wide AVX vector units, without any of the difficulty of writing intrinsics code'
tradeoffs: Separate C-like SPMD language and LLVM-based compiler, not a header library; kernels are called from C/C++ through generated headers; README says it targets the SIMD units of CPUs and Intel GPUs.
caveats: Generic README claim with no workload, CPU, compiler or flags; the detailed performance page (ispc.github.io/perf.html) and the InPar 2012 paper were not reachable here (github.io and ACM blocked). Category fit is weak: it is a compiler that replaces hand-written intrinsics, not an intrinsics library. Tier C until the peer-reviewed paper or an artifact run is checked.
found_via: github.com/topics/simd?l=c%2B%2B page (ispc/ispc listed, 3k stars); README opened via raw.githubusercontent.com

name: avx-512-sort (Bramas)
baseline: std::sort (GNU C++ sort) and Intel IPP sort
workload: Sorting arrays of int, double and int key/value pairs with an AVX-512 partition plus branch-free bitonic small-sort hybrid quicksort on Skylake.
claimed_speedup: About 4x faster than the GNU C++ sort and about 1.4x faster than the Intel IPP library on a Skylake Xeon (paper abstract, arXiv 1704.08579 / IJACSA 2017, seen in a search snippet only)
compiler_and_flags: README lists GCC -mavx512f -mavx512cd -mavx512vl -mavx512bw -mavx512dq for SKL and -march=native; benchmark flags used in the paper not confirmed
hardware: Skylake Xeon (model not confirmed); Knights Landing in the older report
stars_or_usage: 29 stars; paper-linked; same algorithm family is credited by numpy/x86-simd-sort
tradeoffs: Header-only (sort512.hpp, sort512kv.hpp), AVX-512 only (KNL and Skylake-X flag sets), OpenMP parallel variant; an ARM SVE port is referenced on gitlab.inria.fr (not reachable here). Later libraries (x86-simd-sort, Highway vqsort) cover the same space.
caveats: Snippet only: arXiv and the IJACSA page were blocked, and neither the master branch README nor the 'paper' branch (LICENSE and main.cpp only) carries numbers, so the speedups could not be checked against a table. Likely tier B once the peer-reviewed paper is opened. Baseline compiler and flags unknown; only Skylake AVX-512 hardware is covered.
found_via: WebSearch: 'Bramas hybrid quicksort vectorized AVX-512 Skylake speedup over std::sort Intel IPP github'; repo opened on github.com

name: UltraSIMD
baseline: scalar C++ implementations inside the library (benchmark column SpeedupVsScalar)
workload: Dot product, SAXPY, L2, cosine, Hamming and Jaccard distances over F32, F16, I8, BF16 and U8 vectors of 15 to 16384 elements, 175 benchmark rows, AVX-512 path versus scalar path.
claimed_speedup: Repo description: 18.7x via AVX-512. In simd_v3_benchmark_results_1751127313.csv the best row is F32 DotProduct at 8192 elements, 18.67x versus scalar; the later 'fixed' CSV peaks at 16.73x (F32 DotProduct, 4096); other rows are lower (Jaccard 7.57x, Hamming 4.64x, L2 2.04x, cosine 2.03x, SAXPY 1.69x, memory-bandwidth rows 1.0x).
compiler_and_flags: README recommends -O3 -march=native -mtune=native -ffast-math; flags actually used for the CSV runs not stated
hardware: CPU model not stated; CSV lists features AVX512F, FMA, F16C, VNNI
tradeoffs: Header-only, x86-64 only (scalar, AVX2, AVX-512 dispatch), no NEON; ships F16/BF16/I8 types; README calls it production quality but the repo has two commits.
caveats: First-party numbers with no CPU model; the scalar baseline is the library's own scalar path (unknown whether compiled with auto-vectorization or -ffast-math); small vector sizes in cache; headline 18.7x only appears in one of three CSV files and the corrected CSV is lower. Tiny repo with two commits; no comparison with Highway, xsimd or Eigen. Kept as a low-confidence record.
found_via: WebSearch: 'SIMD C++ header-only library README benchmark results "times faster than scalar" AVX2 AVX-512 NEON speedup table compiler flags' (github.com filter); README and three CSV files opened

name: memchr (Rust crate)
baseline: Rust standard library substring search (rust/std/memmem; str::find)
workload: rebar benchmark suite, 53 substring-search benchmarks on x86_64, prebuilt searcher and oneshot (build plus search) classes, geometric mean of speed ratios against the fastest engine.
claimed_speedup: prebuilt: memchr 2.5.0 geometric mean ratio 1.03 versus std 6.50 (std about 6.3x slower, derived from page data); oneshot: memchr 1.04 versus std 5.26 (about 5.1x, derived from page data)
compiler_and_flags: Rust std version 1.73.0-nightly 180dffba1 as the baseline; rustc flags for the recorded run not stated on the pages opened
tradeoffs: Rust-only API (not callable from C++ without a binding); SSE2/AVX2 on x86_64, NEON on aarch64, wasm32 SIMD, SWAR fallback; Unlicense side is a public-domain dedication with no patent grant.
caveats: Baseline is Rust's std, not libc memmem or a C++ library; the README comparison covers substring search (memmem) only. The benchmark machine and rustc flags are not stated in the README or the benchmarks directory listing I opened; results in benchmarks/record/x86_64/2023-08-26.csv. The author is both library and suite author (rebar).
found_via: github.com/topics/simd?l=rust page (BurntSushi/memchr listed, 1.6k stars); README opened via raw.githubusercontent.com

name: EVE (Expressive Vector Engine)
baseline: scalar C++ / compiler auto-vectorization (no baseline stated; successor of Boost.SIMD)
workload: C++20 SIMD wrapper with a math function library for SSE2 to AVX-512, NEON/ASIMD and fixed-size SVE; the repo has a benchmarks/module harness (nanobench) but no published results.
claimed_speedup: No numbers: README says the goal is 'an efficient, low-level, high-abstraction library suited for high performance' and cites three papers (PACT 2012, HPCS 2018, a 2014-era Scalable Computing article) without summarizing results.
tradeoffs: Requires C++20; fixed-size SVE only; marked 'operational' with possible performance issues remaining.
caveats: No benchmark numbers in README; benchmark directory has only the harness (CMakeLists.txt, experiment.hpp, generators.hpp, nanobench.h), no result tables. Documentation and papers live on github.io, ACM and HAL pages that were blocked here. Included as the most notable SIMD library of the category not yet catalogued, to be retiered when the Boost.SIMD/EVE papers or an independent comparison against xsimd/Highway can be opened.
found_via: WebSearch: 'EVE Expressive Vector Engine C++ SIMD library jfalcou paper performance compared to xsimd Highway'; github.com/topics/simd-library; repo and commits pages opened
